title: Jio sets IPO price band at ₹1,065–1,119 for ₹10.3 lakh crore valuation
excerpt: Reliance Industries' digital arm plans to open subscriptions on October 21, aiming to raise about ₹30,200 crore in what would be India's largest-ever IPO — with no offer-for-sale by existing investors.
body:
• Jio Platforms is set to price its IPO at ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 per share, targeting a valuation of as much as ₹10.3 lakh crore (about $107 billion), according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. At the upper end, the issue would raise about ₹30,200 crore. Cash generation underpins the pricing: free cash flow jumped from about ₹1,500 crore in fiscal 2024 to ₹42,000 crore in fiscal 2026, net leverage fell to 0.36 times EBITDA, and Q4 FY26 net profit rose 13 per cent to ₹7,935 crore.
  • The offer is expected to open for anchor investors on October 19, 2026, with public subscription from October 21 to 23 and shares likely to begin trading on October 28, on the BSE and NSE. All terms remain subject to change.
  • Crucially, it is a pure fresh issue of up to 270 million new shares — no offer for sale. Existing backers, including Meta, Google, Silver Lake and KKR, are not selling, so every rupee raised flows into the company, with up to ₹27,500 crore earmarked to repay borrowings at subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm.
  • What it means for you: retail investors need 13 shares per lot, roughly ₹14,547 at the upper band. The grey market premium of about ₹172 (as of October 10) points to an expected listing pop near 15 per cent. Reliance Industries shareholders get indirect upside from the value unlocking.

Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms is closing in on what would be India's largest-ever initial public offering. The telecom and digital services arm of Reliance Industries Ltd. is set to price its shares at ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 apiece, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg, valuing the company at as much as ₹10.3 lakh crore — roughly $107 billion.

At the upper end of the band, the IPO would raise about ₹30,200 crore, according to Bloomberg's calculations, surpassing Hyundai Motor India's ₹27,800 crore share sale in October 2024, currently India's biggest.

Context & Background

Jio filed its draft prospectus with SEBI in June for an offering of as many as 270 million new shares, about 2.93 per cent of post-issue equity. The structure is unusual for a blockbuster listing: there is no offer-for-sale component. Meta, Google, Silver Lake, KKR and sovereign wealth funds that bought in during the 2020 fundraising round are staying put, so the entire proceeds land in the company's account.

The biggest single use of that money is not expansion — it is debt repayment. Per the draft filings, Jio plans to use up to ₹27,500 crore to prepay borrowings at Reliance Jio Infocomm, including dollar- and yen-denominated loans raised for network expansion, with targeted loans topping ₹30,000 crore in outstanding principal.

That deleveraging is partly about optics. Telecom operators are valued like utilities by public markets — capital-hungry, spectrum-dependent businesses — and Jio's management wants investors to see the company as a technology platform. The pitch has substance: Jio today spans broadband, enterprise connectivity, cloud, streaming, payments and increasingly AI infrastructure, employs more than 11,000 people and has filed over 6,800 patents globally. Its subscriber base stood at 524.4 million at the end of March 2026, including 268.5 million 5G users and more than 27 million fixed-broadband subscribers.

Impact & Analysis

The reported valuation is below some earlier expectations. Valuations floated in the $130–170 billion range at one point; Motilal Oswal estimated $115–118 billion in June and Dolat Capital about $110 billion. A sell-off in Indian equities has tempered pricing ambitions — which may actually help the offering, since a more conservatively priced IPO leaves room for a healthy listing-day pop.

The debt-repayment use of proceeds removes foreign-currency exposure and lowers interest costs, setting up a cleaner balance sheet for investment in 5G, fibre, hyperscale data centres and AI infrastructure. Nineteen banks — including Kotak, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and Citigroup — are on the syndicate. The deeper question for investors is whether Jio deserves a telecom multiple or a tech-platform one: telecom still brings in 77 per cent of consolidated revenue, and rival Bharti Airtel's premium-customer strategy gives the market a live comparison.

Diaspora Angle

This is India's primary-market event of the year: the IPO is accessible to non-resident investors through the NRI quota, and foreign portfolio investors will be watching the book-build as a test of demand for large Indian share sales.

What's Next

Deliberations are ongoing, and the price range, valuation and timing could still change. The anchor book is scheduled to open October 19, public subscription runs October 21–23, with listing expected October 28. Watch the subscription numbers across retail, institutional and HNI segments — a blockbuster of this size will absorb significant domestic and foreign liquidity, and its reception will set the tone for the rest of India's IPO pipeline.
